data.title: Japan's Inflation Likely to Rise Much More Next Year — Market Talk
data.description: Japan's inflation is likely to rise much further next year, Capital Economics' Marcel Thieliant says in commentary. Even though the country's inflation excluding fresh food and energy slowed again in October, "we still expect a sharp acceleration in inflation excluding fresh food and energy over the coming months," the head of Asia-Pacific says. The rise in 'other industrial products' inflation has further room to run, he says. "What's more, the producer price data point to an acceleration in food products inflation," Thieliant adds. Capital Economics now expects the BOJ to raise rates to 2.5% by mid-2027. (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

data.title: Asian Equities Fall as Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Fails to Staunch AI Stock Selloff
data.description:
By Ronnie Harui

Asian equities fell Friday morning as Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering failed to staunch the selloff in artificial intelligence stocks.

"The central story was the paradox of a record-breaking AI-sector IPO failing to arrest a broader market selloff," Commerzbank Research analysts said in a report. "Rather than acting as a rising tide, the listing appeared to trigger rotation out of existing AI-related names as investors redeployed capital into the new issue," they said.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, raised about $81 billion in the largest IPO on record, ending the overnight session with a market capitalization of roughly $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic shares opened more than 30% above their $83 IPO price, though gains moderated during the session to finish up 17% at $97.17 in their market debut. The pullback "coincided with declines in other AI-related stocks amid concerns about how higher interest rates affect technology valuations," said Antonio Di Giacomo, senior market analyst at XS.com, in an email.

The SPDR Select Sector Technology exchange-traded fund, which tracks the tech industry group of the U.S.' S&P 500, entered bear-market territory on Thursday, closing 1.9% lower at $160.69, more than 20% below its October peak.

Across Asia, South Korea's Kospi slid 4.7%, with chip-making index heavyweights SK Hynix shedding 6.3% and Samsung Electronics losing 4.8%. Japan's Nikkei Stock Average slipped 4.7%, as AI proxy SoftBank Group fell 15.6%, memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings dropped 12.6%, and Advantest, a manufacturer of automatic test equipment for the semiconductor industry, declined 12.3%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 benchmark index was down 0.9%.

Short-dated Asian and U.S. government bonds rose in price terms Friday morning as the equity-markets' selloff bolstered safe-haven demand for sovereign debt.

Yields on Australia's two-year government bonds declined 4 basis points to 4.6150% and on New Zealand's two-year sovereign notes fell 2 basis points to 3.8740%. U.S. two-year Treasury yields edged 2 basis points lower to 4.7429%% following Thursday's Treasury yield declines. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

"Risk aversion intensified, driving demand for U.S. Treasurys," two strategists at OCBC Group Research said in a report. "Investors continued to unwind crowded positions and reassess the macro outlook as Anthropic's record IPO sharpened scrutiny of stretched AI valuations and financing risks," the strategists added.

Write to Ronnie Harui at ronnie.harui@wsj.com

data.title: China Stock Market Tipped To Open Under Water On Friday
data.description:
BEIJING (dpa-AFX) - The China stock market turned lower again on Thursday, one day after ending the four-day losing streak in which it had slumped almost 100 points or 2.7 percent. The Shanghai Composite Index now sits just beneath the 3,580-point plateau and the losses may accelerate on Friday.

The global forecast for the Asian markets is weak on continuing AI concerns and rising crude oil prices. The European and U.S. markets were down and the Asian bourses are expected to open in similar fashion.

The SCI finished modestly lower on Thursday as losses from the retail, technology, industrial and transportation stocks were offset by gains from the financials and communications companies.

For the day, the index slipped 10.21 points or 0.28 percent to finish at 3,577.62 after trading between 3,547.94 and 3,584.28. The Shenzhen Composite Index dropped 29.71 points or 1.47 percent to end at 1,997.54.

The lead from Wall Street is broadly negative as the major averages opened slightly higher on Thursday but quickly turned lower and continued to accelerate to the downside throughout the session, ending at daily lows.

The Dow plunged 1,101.11 points or 2.19 percent to finish at 49,097.06, while the NASDAQ tumbled 550.69 points or 2.25 percent to close at 23,879.20 and the S&P 500 crashed 147.80 points or 2.02 percent to end at 7,175.83.

The markets initially benefited from a positive reaction to artificial intelligence company Anthropic's (ANT) initial public offering. Buying interest waned shortly after the start of trading, however, and selling pressure intensified soon after intelligence company Anthropic made its debut on the NASDAQ.

While the Claude developer priced its initial public offering at a higher-than-expected $83 per share and soared by nearly 40 percent as it began trading, the stock pulled back well off its highs as the day progressed. The pullback by Anthropic and the sell-off was attributed to profit taking amid lingering concerns about where the AI trade goes from here.

In U.S. economic news, the Labor Department released a report showing first-time claims for U.S. unemployment benefits unexpectedly edged higher last week.

Crude oil prices edged higher on Thursday as fears of supply disruptions increased in the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude for December delivery was up $0.17 or 0.20 percent at $83.43 per barrel.

data.title: China leaves its lending benchmarks unchanged for 18th straight month in November
data.description:
China kept its benchmark lending rates unchanged on Friday for the 18th straight month in November, in line with market expectations.

The one-year loan prime rate (LPR) (CNYLPR1Y=CFXS) was kept at 3.00%, while the five-year LPR (CNYLPR5Y=CFXS) was unchanged at 3.50%.

In a Reuters survey of 28 market participants conducted this week, 23, or 82% of all respondents, predicted that both rates would remain steady.

The other five expected a cut to one or both rates.

Most new and outstanding loans in China are based on the one-year LPR, while the five-year rate influences the pricing of mortgages.

data.title: Australian Permitting a Risk For Lithium Supply Outlook — Market Talk
data.description: UBS remains positive on medium-term lithium prices, in part because of environmental permitting processes in Australia that tend to take longer than expected. The bank looked at 20 mining projects referred to Australia's federal regulator in the past five years and found average permitting time was around 2.5 years versus company expectations of under 1.5 years. It says four lithium projects in Western Australia--accounting for almost 50% of Australian growth to FY 2035, and 13% of global supply growth--are under federal environmental permitting review. That poses "risks to both company and market expectations on timelines for medium term supply ramp up," it says. Equities look cheap "for those who can tolerate near term volatility," says UBS, highlighting IGO and Wildcat as top picks. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; @RhiannonHoyle)

data.title: Australia shares slide to one-month low as weak data hits banks, miners
data.description:
Australian shares fell to a one-month low on Friday, pressured by financials and miners a day after weak jobs data fuelled fears of a sharper-than-expected economic slowdown and raised expectations of rate cuts next year.

The S&P/ASX 200 index was down 1% at 8,639.4 points, as of 2322 GMT, its lowest level since October 15. Earlier in the day, it had fallen as much as 1.5% to its lowest intraday level since mid-June.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that the jobless rate unexpectedly jumped to a five-year high of 4.9% in October, while employment registered a sharp fall.

The reading heightened concerns about the impact of the Reserve Bank of Australia's five rate hikes this year, prompting investors to scale back bets on further tightening and price in a rate cut by mid-2027.

"It (RBA) will also likely face growing criticism that it might have 'overcooked' the economy via tightening too much this year," said Andrew Ticehurst, senior economist at Nomura Australia.

Financials headed for their worst week since mid-August, with a 0.8% drop on the day as investors focused on the implications of a cooling labour market for credit quality and lending growth.

All the "Big Four" banks fell between 1% and 2%.

Miners slipped 1%, extending their losing streak to a seventh session as copper prices hovered near a seven-month low.

Shares of bellwether stock BHP dipped 0.3%.

Gold stocks tumbled 2.2%, on track to hit their lowest level in more than three months, after bullion sank to a 14-month low.

Northern Star and Evolution Mining slid 5.7% and 2.5%, respectively.

Tech stocks slumped 4.3%, tracking losses in US peers after Anthropic's super-sized IPO did not revive faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence.

New Zealand's benchmark S&P/NZX 50 index fell 0.6% to 14,160.95 points and has lost 0.1% so far this week.

data.title: Japan Tobacco Shares Slump After $8.6 Billion Hit From Russia Business
data.description:
By Kosaku Narioka

Japan Tobacco shares fell sharply early Friday after the company projected an $8.6 billion hit stemming from the loss of control over its Russian operations.

Shares recently traded 9.0% lower at 5,329 yen, equivalent to $33.37, in Tokyo.

The Japanese tobacco maker said late Thursday that it would book a loss of 1.377 trillion yen, equivalent to $8.62 billion, as a result of losing control of the Russian business.

Earlier this month, Japan Tobacco reported that all seven of its Russian entities were placed under temporary administration by a Russian company under orders from President Vladimir Putin.

Japan Tobacco projected a net loss of Y724.00 billion for 2026, reversing its previous net-profit view owing primarily to the special loss related to the Russian business. The company also cut its dividend forecast for this year to Y204 a share from Y272.

The tobacco maker said it remained confident it could raise dividends in the coming years, supported by profit growth.

Japan Tobacco had expected Russia to account for about 10% of its revenue and 25% of adjusted operating profit in 2026.

The tobacco maker has the ability to generate strong profit and cash flow in markets other than Russia, but its creditworthiness could be weighed by a big loss and lower profitability due to the removal of the Russian business from consolidated reporting, said Yasuaki Kudamatsu, senior credit analyst at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.

Write to Kosaku Narioka at kosaku.narioka@wsj.com

data.title: RBA board member sees pockets of strong demand in economy, weakness elsewhere
data.description:
An Australian central bank board member said on Friday that she sees pockets of strong demand in the economy but weakness elsewhere set against a global oil supply shock that has made policymaking more difficult.

Speaking at an event in Canberra, Renee Fry-McKibbin, an external board member at the Reserve Bank of Australia, said trade-offs in monetary policy are difficult and board members can disagree on how to manage them in part because they prefer different objectives, inflation or employment.

"This is the situation we are in now, with pockets of strong demand in Australia, and weakness elsewhere overlaid with a massive global oil supply shock following the conflict in the Middle East," Fry-McKibbin said.

The RBA has raised interest rates five times this year but its latest move to lift rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% came after a split board decision, with three members concerned the economy was nearing a sharp downturn. A surprise rise in the unemployment rate to 4.9% added to those worries as markets bet rates had peaked.

"Balancing central bank mandates requires judgement. Judgements are made amid uncertainty, incomplete information, and lags in policy effects, yet decisions still need to be made," she said.

She added the board was watching the economic implications of AI very closely and how it could help inform policy decisions.

data.title: Funds dump copper but Shanghai has run out of metal: Andy Home
data.description:
By Andy Home

It's been an eventful week for Doctor Copper.

Fund sellers have hammered the copper market on both sides of the Atlantic as the AI trade unwinds, the dollar rises and economic uncertainty builds.

London Metal Exchange (LME) three-month copper slumped 6% to a seven-month low of $12,379.50 per metric ton on Wednesday.

Yet, just 48 hours earlier, the Shanghai Futures Exchange (ShFE) contract was in the grip of an unprecedented squeeze as available stocks were insufficient to cover delivery commitments.

Financial futures have disconnected from fundamentals, but the fundamentals are also geographically fractured thanks to the US tariff trade.

This is copper in the quantum age, a confusing cacophony of conflicting signals.

AI ROLLER-COASTER

It's no coincidence that tin has been the other clear loser among the LME base metals pack this week, with three-month metal tumbling to an eight-month low of $41,035 per ton.

Both copper and tin rode the AI investment wave to all-time highs earlier this year thanks to their usage in data centers as wiring and circuit-board solder, respectively.

The AI bull narrative may be rooted in reality but it's been dosed with a good deal of hyperscaler hype.

Popular pushback on new AI data centers and the promise of more regulatory scrutiny by a Democratic-controlled Congress have punctured the bubble in both AI technology stocks and "internet" metals such as copper, tin and silver.

As AI expectations get scaled back, attention is turning to the impact of higher central bank rates on non-AI manufacturing activity and what is already soft copper demand.

Analysts at Citi estimate global copper usage grew by a highly modest 0.8% year-on-year in August with weak domestic consumption in China acting as the main drag.

SHANGHAI SQUEEZE

Lacklustre demand was no comfort for short-position holders on the ShFE November contract earlier this week.

The November contract spiked by over 9% to 118,060 yuan per ton on Monday, the day of its expiry. The spread over the December contract exploded to over 10,000 yuan per ton at one stage.

There were simply not enough warranted stocks to cover short positions. Total ShFE deliverable inventory has collapsed from a March peak of 433,458 tons to 27,642 tons. The amount available for settlement of November contracts was just 2,270 tons.

Low exchange stocks speak to genuine tightness in the Chinese market. Domestic premiums are elevated and the Yangshan premium (SMM-CUYP-CN), a closely monitored gauge of import demand assessed by Shanghai Metals Market, has jumped to a record $360 per ton over the LME price.

Tight raw materials markets have slowed domestic production of refined metal. China's copper output this year is expected to grow at the slowest pace in decades.

Meanwhile, imports of refined copper fell by 12.5% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026.

China, the world's largest copper buyer, has found itself in unexpected competition for units with the United States thanks to a US delivery premium predicated on expectations of import tariffs.

COMPETITION

The White House has maintained a studious silence on the subject but until very recently the US was the market of first resort for any available copper.

The country's imports surged by 80% year-on-year to 1.64 million tons in 2025, according to the World Bureau of Metal Statistics, which collects official customs data. Imports rose by 10% to 1.31 million tons in the first eight months of 2026.

Shanghai short-position holders now find themselves where London shorts were in August, when the premium for cash metal over three-month delivery (CMCU0-3) soared to $545 per ton.

That was also due to low exchange stocks.

The amount of metal on LME warrant has increased from under 100,000 tons to 291,925 tons since August, largely reflecting deliveries at US ports as it became more profitable to warrant the metal on the LME than to customs-clear and deliver it to a CME warehouse.

It's now China's turn to feel the squeeze caused by the gravitational pull exerted by the tariff trade.

The problem facing Shanghai shorts is that stocks are much lower and available LME units are still heavily concentrated in the US rather than at closer Asian locations.

TARIFF TEST

The CME copper premium has contracted sharply in recent weeks. Indeed, on a spot basis, the CME is now trading at a discount to the LME.

The implication is that the market is increasingly less sure that the US will impose tariffs in the wake of the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections.

The default position laid out in the Department of Commerce's 2025 report on US import dependency was for a 15% tariff to be introduced at the start of 2027, rising to 30% in 2028.

The irony is that if copper starts leaving the US for China, it may make tariffs more likely as the White House looks to keep hold of its newly acquired stockpile.

($1 = 6.6702 Chinese yuan renminbi)

(The opinions expressed here are those of Andy Home, a columnist for Reuters.)
